title: Anaesthetic management of a pregnant patient undergoing meningioma resection: A case report
case_prompt: A 28-year-old primigravida at 29 weeks’ gestation experienced a 3-minute generalized tonic–clonic seizure in the community and was brought to the emergency department. On arrival, her consciousness had returned to baseline. She denied headache or visual symptoms. Her blood pressure and other vital signs were within normal limits. Physical and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Her pregnancy history had been uncomplicated, with no prior medical or family history of seizures or neurologic disease. Laboratory investigations, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were normal. Obstetric ultrasound confirmed a single live fetus in cephalic presentation without placental or amniotic fluid abnormalities. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed a 5.3 by 3.2 cm extra-axial dural-based mass overlying the left frontal and temporal lobes, with moderate mass effect. She was started on dexamethasone and levetiracetam and admitted for observation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Eclampsia was excluded because of the absence of hypertension and neurologic prodromes — “She had no headache or visual symptoms and therefore eclampsia was not deemed a likely cause for her presentation.”  
2. Epilepsy was considered given her tonic–clonic seizure, but she had no prior history of seizures — “Of the neurological causes, important causes to consider are epilepsy, eclampsia, intracranial infection, trauma, cerebral-venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial malignancy…”  
3. Intracranial infection was considered but ruled out by normal laboratory investigations — “Laboratory investigations were normal.”  
4. Trauma was deemed unlikely in the absence of any head-injury history — “Of the neurological causes, important causes to consider are epilepsy, eclampsia, intracranial infection, trauma…”  
5. Cerebral-venous sinus thrombosis was in the differential but imaging did not demonstrate venous occlusion — “Of the neurological causes, important causes to consider are … cerebral-venous sinus thrombosis…”  
6. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome associated with HELLP syndrome was considered but there was no evidence of HELLP or hypertension — “… as well as rarer causes such as posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome associated with HELLP syndrome.”  
7. Intracranial malignancy, specifically a dural-based lesion, became most likely based on MRI features — “MRI brain revealed a 5.3 by 3.2 cm extra-axial dural-based mass consistent with meningioma.”
